title: A scientometric analysis and review of spatial cognition studies within the framework of neuroscience and architecture
review_question: To investigate main research themes and developments in spatial cognition research over the past two decades (1999–2019) on the basis of a keyword co-occurrence analysis of published articles, and to examine the current focus of research at the intersection of neuroscience studies on spatial cognition and architecture and how this area can evolve in the future.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Bibliometric data retrieved from ISI Web of Science (Science Citation Index Expanded, Social Sciences Citation Index, Arts & Humanities Citation Index) for the term 'spatial cognition' in keywords, abstracts, and titles. Search period 1999-2019. Manual screening excluded papers not related to spatial cognition research. For the neuroscience and architecture intersection, key empirical papers were reviewed, excluding viewpoint or purely theoretical studies without verifiable observation.

synthesis_conclusions: The study revealed main research themes and their relations in spatial cognition, as well as connections between spatial cognition and architecture.

There is a strong natural link between neuroscience and architecture, but a gap exists between the constructs, terminologies, and research methods of architects/architectural researchers and neuroscience researchers.
Embodied spatial cognition and affordances of architectural design provide a robust framework to guide further investigation in this area.
Earlier works on spatial cognition focused on left-right reversal, mirror reversal, and mirror vision, while latest projects focus on cognitive cartography, eye tracking, SNARC, and mobility.

Future studies should investigate human experience of architecture more holistically, incorporating multisensory spatial information and relevant contextual variables beyond the current visual-centric focus.
evidence_gaps: A gap is observed between the constructs, terminologies, and research methods of architecture and neuroscience.
There is a lack of systematic theoretical and empirical frameworks in the field of neuroscience and architecture.
Existing research at the intersection of neuroscience and architecture relies merely on visual information, often 2D images, neglecting embodied and multisensory cognition.
A theory of affordances is missing in the field of architecture.
There is a huge unexplored area at the intersection of embodied spatial cognition and architecture to test hypotheses about their mutual impacts.

Many studies in the field are based on assumptions about design characteristics and their effects on people, reflecting prior observations and 'common sense' knowledge rather than scientific verification.
limitations: The report focused only on spatial cognition studies within the neuroscience domain, acknowledging that neuroscience research can be utilized in architecture in many other ways.

The body of evidence reviewed for the intersection of neuroscience and architecture relies heavily on visual stimuli, often 2D images, limiting understanding of embodied and multisensory human-built environment interaction.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The hippocampus forms a cognitive map of the environment, which is crucial for spatial memory, navigation, and learning. This paper extends the theory by examining how architectural features influence the formation and utilization of these cognitive maps.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural features are perceived, leading to specific patterns of hippocampal neural activity that contribute to the formation and updating of cognitive maps, which in turn support various spatial cognitive functions.

steps.from_construct: Environmental architectural features (e.g., layout, ceiling height, visual cues)
steps.to_construct: Sensory perception and processing of spatial information
